title: Interracial Publics
source: Current Anthropology

extra.summary: This article examines the formation of “interracial publics” in postapartheid South Africa, showing how race, intimacy, and belonging are negotiated through mediated encounters. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork, interviews, and media analysis, it traces how relationships between people historically classified as “white” and “nonwhite” become publicly visible and collectively interpreted across print, broadcast, and digital platforms. These publics are ambivalent and contested: they can normalize formerly forbidden intimacies and foster cross-racial connection, yet they also reinscribe racialized hierarchies through gendered and sexualized discourse. Situating these dynamics within South Africa’s longer histories of settler colonialism and apartheid, the article argues that the regulation of intimacy has been central to projects of racial governance and white supremacy and continues to animate their afterlives in contemporary struggles over visibility, belonging, and desire. Interracial intimacy functions as both a measure and a mediator of contemporary racial formations, contributing to comparative anthropological debates on race, media, affect, and the public sphere in postcolonial societies.

title: Destabilizing citizenship: De-documentation and the politics of disenchantment
source: Anthropological Theory
affiliation: University of California, Irvine; Irvine University

extra.summary: Drawing on recent critiques of liberal conceptions of legal-juridical citizenship, this article develops a model of disenchanted citizenship that moves away from treating legal-juridical citizenship as an unqualified good, normative value, or universal concept. Building on the concept of the regionally specific citizenship regime, constructions of citizenship that can be bound within one nation-state or extend across several, the article examines the inequalities, instabilities, and exclusions that remain central to contemporary regional constructions of citizenship. By offering new language to describe old and new processes of de-documentation, the review and revocation of core identity documents, and de-citizenship, the revocation of birthright or naturalized citizenship, the essay explores how citizenship remains a site of bio-documentary power, the power to make and unmake populations through the production, interrogation, destabilization, and even destruction of digital and physical files and documents.

title: A closer look at the postcranial skeleton of Omo I from the Kibish Formation, Ethiopia: points of divergence from recent humans
source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute

extra.summary: Previous studies have described the postcranial skeleton of Omo I as anatomically modern yet have often noted features in its anatomy that are unusual in comparison to recent humans. The present study presents an analysis of linear measurements of many portions of the skeleton in comparison to several samples of recent (Holocene) humans. Special attention is paid to contrasts with Zulu males, a sample that approximates Omo I in overall size. The results show that Omo I has a long humerus with a slender shaft, a proximally positioned ulnar tuberosity, a short olecranon process, large articular ends and flattened proximal articular surface of the first metacarpal, a large acetabulum, a narrow patellar notch, and a low talus with a long neck. These join the set of distinctive features identified in previous analyses and combine to push the skeleton away from recent humans in multivariate space. A few of the features appear to be plesiomorphic, others apomorphic and ‘modern’, and some possibly idiosyncratic. Close inspection of the unusual dimensions suggests that some are unreliable, including the original estimate for humeral length. This implies that Omo I had a stout rather than linear build.

title: Gough's Cave and biomolecular archaeology: a story of evolving interpretation
source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute

extra.summary: Gough's Cave is a key archaeological site that has been at heart of British archaeology for the past century. Professor Chris Stringer, whom this special issue honours, has been a key figure in excavations and research projects at the site for many decades. Here, I detail how the ever‐increasing weight of biomolecular data generation over the past 50 years, which includes radiocarbon dating, dietary isotope, and ancient DNA analysis, has resulted in an ever‐evolving interpretation of the two oldest and most archaeologically significant assemblages at the site: the Mesolithic skeleton of Cheddar Man (between 10,600 and 9,900 years ago), and the large post‐glacial deposit attributed to the Magdalenian culture (between 15,100 and 14,300 years ago).

title: Affective boundaries: a computational analysis of topic dynamics and sentiment in online reactions to Seoul's Filipino domestic worker pilot programme
source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies
affiliation: Nanjing University; Yonsei University; National Chengchi University; University of Hong Kong

extra.summary: In 2024, the Seoul Metropolitan Government launched the Foreign Housekeeping Managers Pilot Project, employing Filipino domestic workers to address care labour shortages amid low fertility and aging. As Korea's first formal institutionalisation of migrant care work, it offers a rare chance to observe how public commenters on Naver, the country's dominant news portal, interpret and contest this change. Using a mixed-methods computational approach combining manual topic classification, LDA topic modelling, and deep learning-based sentiment analysis, we analyse 543 news articles and 20,685 comments from September 2024 to April 2025. Seven themes appeared: working conditions and wages, policy rollout, public reactions, international comparisons, migrant rights concerns, the programme as a response to care shortages and fertility decline, and alternative models. Sentiment skewed heavily negative, dominated by anger and disgust tied to perceived unfairness and contested belonging. Fluctuations tracked policy events, showing how administrative developments became political flashpoints. We use the concept of affective boundary-making, advanced as a synthesis of symbolic boundary work and affective publics rather than as a new theoretical construct, to describe how anger and disgust function as the medium through which deservingness boundaries are drawn during the pre-institutional phase of a care-migration policy.

title: Empowerment Beyond Inclusion: Uneven Impacts of Community-Based Tourism in Vietnam’s Mountainous Regions
source: World Development Sustainability
affiliation: Vietnam National University, Hanoi; The University of Sydney

extra.summary: While Community-Based Tourism (CBT) is widely championed for rural development, its capacity to deliver equitable empowerment remains heavily contested. This study empirically evaluates the multidimensional impacts of CBT across economic, social, cultural, and environmental dimensions in Northwest Vietnam, identifying the structural determinants of its sustainability impacts. Utilising survey data from 211 ethnic minority households, the study employs Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) to test the effects of six key determinants: community empowerment, women's empowerment, household capacity, financial access, ethnic identity, and CBT value chain retention. The results reveal a critical decoupling between community level gains and stagnant household level benefits. Crucially, community organisational empowerment emerges as the sole consistent driver across all four sustainability pillars, proving that cultural and environmental assets function as collective goods requiring robust local governance. Conversely, individual household capacities, ethnic attachment, and subsidised financial credit largely fail to produce sustainability outcomes. Furthermore, the study uncovers a profound gender empowerment paradox: while external support elevates women into public leadership, it fails to dismantle intra-household patriarchal structures. title: Land Use Restrictions and Livelihood Resilience in Ethnic Minority Communities Around the Giant Panda National Park, China: A Configurational Analysis
source: Land

extra.summary: Protected areas increasingly reshape land use rules, resource accessibility, and livelihood opportunities for adjacent communities. However, household livelihood resilience under protected-area land use restrictions is rarely explained by a single factor; rather, it is better understood through the combined configurations of spatial constraint intensity, natural-capital dependence, social capital, and alternative livelihood capacity. Taking households in five sampled Yi, Qiang, and Hui villages around the Giant Panda National Park in China as empirical cases, this study examines the configurational relationships through which land use restrictions are associated with household livelihood resilience. Based on survey data from 200 households in five sampled Yi, Qiang, and Hui villages, supplemented by participatory rural appraisal and semi-structured interviews, we apply fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis to identify configurations associated with both high and low livelihood resilience. The results identify two robust high-resilience pathways: an opportunity conversion pathway characterized by weak spatial constraints and strong alternative livelihood capacity, and a dual-capacity support pathway in which social capital and alternative livelihood capacity jointly support livelihood resilience under natural-capital dependence. source: Review of International Business and Strategy

extra.summary: Purpose This paper aims to investigate the business ownership style (BOS) of Indigenous Hui entrepreneurs in the Ningxia Autonomous Region of China as a distinctive system of ethical governance embedded within privately owned enterprise (POE) structures. This study examines how moral reasoning, oral tradition and community-based trust mechanisms become institutionalised as operational domestic and international business practices Design/methodology/approach Drawing upon ethnological fieldwork conducted between 2022 and 2024, including interviews, participant observation, oral testimony and student engagement across Ningxia, this study analyses Hui BOS as a historically grounded yet adaptive model of enterprise governance. The research integrates institutional analysis with ethnological inquiry to examine how Hui entrepreneurs sustain trust, legitimacy and resilience across contemporary market conditions. The reliability of the scale was assessed through internal consistency reliability, split-half reliability, and test–retest reliability. The validity of the scale was evaluated through both content validity and structural validity. title: Ethnic narratives in Dunhuang Bianwen: a digital humanities approach to pluralistic integration
source: Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

extra.summary: As a representative form of folk storytelling and singing literature in the Tang Dynasty, Dunhuang Bianwen emerged in the multi-ethnic borderland of northwest China. It directly reflects the perceptions of ethnic interactions in folk society and possesses significant research value. Guided by the ethnic boundary theory, this study takes the 78 Bianwen texts recorded in the Collected Works of Dunhuang Bianwen (Wang et al., 1957). It constructs a quantitative model integrating three core indicators—Interaction Density, Emotional Orientation, and Interaction Impact intensity—and Standard History Narrative Distance Coefficient, analyzing the interactions between the Han ethnic group and surrounding ethnic minorities including the Turks and Tibetans. This research reveals the narrative essence of “differences exist in interactions while connections are sustained through differences” within the pluralistic integration pattern of the Chinese nation, and offers an interdisciplinary analytical paradigm for relevant studies.

title: From the sacred to the secular: modern transformation of Dai settlement heritages from material, spiritual and social perspectives
source: Journal of Cultural Heritage Management and Sustainable Development
affiliation: Beijing Jiaotong University; Delft University of Technology; Oklahoma State University; Oklahoma State University Oklahoma City

extra.summary: Purpose This study aims to establish a theoretical framework to explore the generation and evolution of Dai settlements in Xishuangbanna, Yunnan Province. The study of Dai settlements is essential for comprehending, preserving and developing the Dai ethnic cultural heritages amid rapid modernization. Design/methodology/approach This article examines the traditional villages in Xishuangbanna, Yunnan Province, China, with a focus on Dai settlements and dwellings from the 1980s to the present, employing a multidisciplinary approach consisting of theoretical analysis, field research and graphic interpretation. Findings This study investigates the material, spiritual and social dimensions that have shaped the formation and evolution of the Dai villages amid modernization. By analyzing two representative spatial cases, it illustrates that Dai villages emerged from a dynamic interplay among multiple dimensions, with varying degrees of impact at every stage. Originality/value This three-dimensional analytical framework offers a deeper understanding of rural settlements from both internal and external perspectives. It provides theoretical insights and practical guidance for architects, planners and policymakers engaged in cultural heritage conservation and rural revitalization.

title: Fluvial Dreams of Modernity: Hydropower Infrastructure, Global Networks, and State Making in Xikang, 1939–1947
source: Twentieth-Century China

extra.summary: Abstract : When China’s Republican government fled to Chongqing during the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937–1945), it brought with it a heightened demand for electricity production for the war effort. The relocation of the Nationalist government and an ambitious new generation of Chinese technocrats to Sichuan Province brought unprecedented resources to West China. After Xikang Province was formally established in 1939, the provincial government under Liu Wenhui acted as a key intermediary that connected the central government’s desire for wartime resources with Xikang elites and officials’ interest in local energy development projects. This new alignment of interests allowed the Xikang provincial government to secure the technical expertise, finances, and equipment necessary to build two state-of-the-art hydropower dams during the wartime period. The legacies of these projects and the engineering experts who worked on them were foundational to the earliest imaginings of the vast scale and potential of hydroelectricity in the Sino-Tibetan borderland.

title: The green nexum: Collateral, clan finance and the moral economy of repo markets
source: Economy and Society

extra.summary: This paper analyses the attempted greening of repurchase agreement (repo) markets through the figure of the ‘green nexum’. Repos are not green in themselves: collateral normally matters insofar as it is liquid, eligible and reusable. Drawing on critical macro-finance, social studies of finance and anthropological theories of exchange, the paper argues that repo markets are not neutral financial ‘plumbing’ but a Braudelian antimarket: an elite, state-entangled formation above ordinary market exchange. The circulation of collateral produces a distinct sociality, binding dealer banks, central banks and asset managers into ranked chains of obligation. Based on fieldwork in international industry standard-setting forums, green-finance training and interviews, the paper shows how green repo attempts to moralize, yet reproduces, collateral-based finance.
